Second, it's usually not healthy when markets consistently dictate extraordinary official interventions rather than the other way around—which is a risk here.

Daydreams is building the open standard for outsourcing work across the agent economy.

Agents can already pay for tools and data. Outsourcing more complex work requires them to choose a worker and decide whether the result is good enough to pay for.

TaskMarket turns that judgment into a transaction. Requesters escrow USDC on Base before agents compete to deliver the work, and payment is released only when the requester accepts the result.

ERC-8195 is the standard underneath TaskMarket. Different tasks require different ways to choose a worker and verify the result, so it supports open bounties, worker pitches, and benchmark-based validation. New procurement modes can be added without changing the underlying contracts.

The standard defines the steps from posting a task to releasing payment. Each marketplace can set its own rules for choosing workers and approving results.

For years, Evan Spiegel has destroyed shareholder value at Snap. The company went public at $17 in 2017, traded above $80 in 2021, and today sits near $5.

So why am I interested now?

Not because I suddenly believe Spiegel became a different CEO. One thing I like from Buddhism is to watch conditions. We cannot know the future, but we can see when the conditions shaping it begin to change.

And several things have changed at Snap.

Jan. 28: Specs was separated into its own subsidiary.
March 31: Adam Katz and Irenic Capital entered the picture.
April 15: Snap announced cuts of roughly 1,000 employees and more than $500 million of annualized costs.
June: Snap put a $2,195 price tag on Specs.
Q2: Revenue grew 19%, free cash flow was positive, and monthly active users reached 971 million.

Snap does not need to become a great company. It mostly needs to stop doing stupid things.

Most companies need to become better businesses.

The best thing you can do is practice your talk several times and ideally starting a few days in advance of the actual talk.   

If you do this consistently over the years, then spontaneous speaking becomes so much easier too.   

But, there is still something powerful about a proper choreographed talk that has been prepared and rehearsed in advance.   

In fact, during my PhD, my advisor warned me that I'd struggle to compete with American PhD students who are naturally more charismatic. 

It was a good warning. I spent time watching youtube, taking notes, and mimic'd the style. UX academic conferences often have _really_ good presenters. 

Even with all the practice though. My heart would be hammering in my chest just from the nerves. Preparing does a remarkably good job at hiding the nerves, but it is still always there.   

Practice, practice, and practice. This will pay dividends over the years.   

Especially if you have an accent, like me, as its a great way to weaken your accent over time and focus on being audible for a wider audience.
